                                         AARP'S STATEMENT OF POSITION

                   AARP, by and through its undersigned counsel, respectfully submits the following

        Statement of Position in the above-mentioned Cause. AARP is the nation’s largest nonprofit,

        nonpartisan organization dedicated to empowering people 50 and older to choose how they live as

        they age. With a nationwide presence, AARP strengthens communities and advocates for what

        matters most to the more than 100 million Americans 50-plus and their families: health security,

        financial stability, and personal fulfillment. AARP has approximately 400,000 members residing

        in Oklahoma representing all segments of the socio-economic scale. AARP has offices in all 50

        states and 3 territories. A substantial percentage of AARP’s members live on fixed or limited

        incomes and depend on reliable low-cost electric service for economic security, health, and

        personal welfare.

                   AARP has carefully reviewed the application, testimony, and responses to data requests

        provided by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”) in this Cause. AARP supports

        OG&E's stated intention of ensuring that large load customers pay the costs fairly allocable to

        them and commit to a minimum term of service, consistent with the requirements established with

        the enactment of Oklahoma House Bill 2992.1 AARP also supports OG&E's stated intention to

        protect its existing customers from the risks and costs associated with serving extra large load

        customers by incorporating appropriate provisions in its proposed Extra Large Power and Light

        (“XLPL”) Tariff and the accompanying Terms and Conditions of Service for Extra Large Load

        Customers (“T&CXLLC”).2 Several provisions of the proposal are meaningful protections for

        residential customers, and AARP identifies and supports them below. However, AARP's review

        identified several areas in which the durability and completeness of OG&E's intended protection

        to existing customers have not yet been demonstrated or can be improved. AARP's

        recommendations below aim to identify and address these gaps with the aim of more completely

        achieving the intended protections articulated by OG&E in this Cause.


                                                   Summary

                1.     As to the Customer Affordability Charge, the Commission should (a) approve the
        charge and the companion Reservation Charge, and (b) require OG&E to specify the crediting
        mechanism, including interval, allocation, bill presentation, and carrying charges, and the
        disposition of any accumulated balance if the charge is later modified or terminated. AARP
        opposes the recommendations of other parties that the charge be eliminated, and submits that its
        proceeds should be applied to the programs against which the charge was calculated rather than
        disbursed without regard to them.

                2.      The Commission should require that the Customer Class Protection Charge be
        given a defined methodology, a defined adversity threshold, a filing interval independent of
        OG&E’s discretion to initiate a rate case, an allocation of the burden of proof to OG&E, and audit
        rights, and should require OG&E to file a cost-of-service study for the XLPL class on a date
        certain. AARP supports PUD’s recommendation that the cost of new generation be allocated to
        the XLPL class to the extent it is caused by XLPL load, rather than averaged across all classes
        with the Company’s embedded fleet, and the Attorney General’s recommendation that class
        allocation factors be updated more frequently. The Attorney General’s recommendation that the
        fail-safe analysis be governed by defined parameters and a clear methodology should likewise be
        adopted.

                3.      The proceeds of the proposed Customer Class Protection Charge should be placed
        in a regulatory liability to be credited to non-XLPL customers. Those proceeds should be subject
        to the same crediting and carrying-charge requirements described in Recommendation 1.

                4.     The Commission should require a deferral mechanism capturing adverse rate
        impacts arising between general rate cases, with carrying charges for the benefit of the impacted
        classes. AARP supports PUD’s proposed annual Customer Impact Assessment and its adoption as
        new Section 515 of the T&CXLLC, with the single modification that deferred balances accrue
        carrying charges.

               5.       OG&E should avoid suggesting that its proposal will benefit existing customers by
        reducing the average cost to serve each customer, implying that adding large loads will generate
        economies of scale. The Commission should decline to accept any such characterization absent
        the quantification OG&E has not performed. The Attorney General’s witness reaches the same
        conclusion, finding the Company’s modified cost-of-service analysis misleading because it added
        load without adding cost.

                6.      In monitoring and calculating the fees and charges to be levied on XLPL customers
        that are intended to protect other customers from the impact of adding the very large loads, OG&E
        should explicitly include those potential stranded asset costs and risks that occur after the
        expiration of its Electric Service Agreement (“ESA”) or after the XLPL customer has exercised
        the right to reduce or terminate its ESA, and should be made financially responsible for the correct
        calculation of those amounts. AARP also supports the Attorney General’s recommendation that
        XLPL customers pre-fund the portion of future network transmission upgrades necessary to
        prevent an increase in transmission costs allocated to other classes, and PUD’s recommendation
        that CIAC-funded infrastructure be explicitly excluded from rate base.

               7.    As to collateral, the Commission should (a) require collateral equal to 100% of
        Minimum Charges for the Initial Term, (b) exclude money market funds from the definition of
        “Cash Equivalent,” and (c) exclude “coin or” from the definition of “Cash.”

                8.      Competitive bidding should continue to be required in procurement unless OG&E
        can demonstrate that timing or cost constraints justify an exception, and Section 4.01(a) of the
        form ESA, which waives competitive bidding for interim capacity, should be struck or bounded.
        OIEC’s witness identifies the same provision as evidence that OG&E may commit to serve a new
        extra large load without demonstrating that it has the resources to serve it.

                9.     OG&E should explicitly specify how it will determine the appropriate discount rate
        to apply in calculating the 30-year Net Present Value of Customer Cost (“NPVCC”) in its
        Integrated Resource Planning (“IRP”) preferred portfolio analysis.3 AARP supports PUD’s
        recommendation that the requested regulatory asset for portfolio optimization software be denied
        in this Cause and the issue taken up in Cause No. PUD 2026-000067.

               10.      The Commission should direct that a Bring Your Own Generation or self-supply
        option be established for XLPL customers. Generation that a large load procures for itself is
        generation that OG&E does not build, and capacity that OG&E does not build, cannot become a
        stranded infrastructure cost borne by the remaining classes. Every other party to address the
        question recommends such an option. AARP asks that two conditions attach: that election of self-
        supply not relieve a customer of the Customer Affordability Charge, the Customer Class Protection

        continues to take; and that any generation-related charge offset extend only to load actually backed
        by accredited capacity meeting Southwest Power Pool resource adequacy and planning reserve
        margin obligations.

                11.    Approval of a single form Electric Service Agreement should not displace review
        of the agreements actually executed. The Commission should condition approval on OG&E
        providing each executed Electric Service Agreement to PUD and to the parties in advance of
        service, subject to the protective order, with an opportunity to seek Commission review.

                                                     Detailed Analysis

        1.        THE CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE SHOULD BE APPROVED, AND THE MECHANISM
                  FOR DELIVERING ITS BENEFIT TO RESIDENTIAL CUSTOMERS SHOULD BE SPECIFIED NOW .

                  a. AARP supports the Customer Affordability Charge and the Reservation Charge.

                  Unlike the Customer Class Protection Charge, the Customer Affordability Charge is set at

        a stated rate of $2.50 per kW-month at both service levels and applies from the outset. The

        companion Reservation Charge applies the same rate against Maximum Contract Demand from

        execution of a Preliminary Agreement until service commences, so that benefit begins to accrue

        before the load energizes and during a period in which OG&E is already incurring cost. AARP

        supports both charges and urges the Commission to approve them.

                  With that said, AARP's support is grounded in what the charge is represented to fund. Mr.

        Shoop testifies that the amount collected approximates the total of the Company's Low Income

        Assistance Program, an expanded Senior Discount for all residential customers who qualify as

        senior citizens, and approximately twenty percent of the residential energy efficiency program.4

        However, OG&E has not committed to that result. When asked to explain how its workpapers

        demonstrate an expanded Senior Discount, OG&E responded only that the relevant tab "includes

        senior citizens from all rates and not just the time-of-use rates."5 When asked whether it considered

        way possible for customers," and, most telling, that "[u]ltimately, the Commission will decide how

        these funds are used."6 The expanded Senior Discount is thus only a theoretical possibility of the

        charge's potential calculation, not an obligation of the tariff. AARP asks that the possibility be

        made binding.

                b. There is presently no mechanism to deliver the benefit.

                Customer Affordability Charge and Reservation Charge revenues are to be credited to a

        regulatory liability. Beyond that, nothing has been specified. PUD asked OG&E to state, among

        other things, “[h]ow the amounts will be reflected in residential customers' bills (as a credit, a rate

        reduction, or otherwise).” OG&E answered subparts (a) through (d) of that request and did not

        respond to subpart (e).7 Asked separately which residential customers will receive the credit, at

        what interval it would be provided, how it will appear on customer bills, and what other credit

        design considerations have been made, OG&E responded that subparts (i) through (iii) “will be

        determined in a future proceeding,” and that “OG&E does not have any other credit design

        considerations at this time.”8

                A charge that collects from XLPL customers beginning on the first day of service, credited

        to a liability with no defined distribution interval, no allocation methodology, no bill presentation,

        and no carrying charges, and held until a general rate case whose timing OG&E controls, is not

        yet a benefit to residential customers. AARP recommends the Commission require OG&E to

        specify, as a condition of approval, (i) the interval at which amounts will be distributed, (ii) the

        regulatory liability accrue carrying charges for the benefit of residential customers, (v) the

                 Every other party to address the charge finds it deficient as filed, though they propose

        different remedies. The Attorney General’s witness observes that “the Company did not indicate

                AARP’s position differs from each of these. The defect some of these witnesses identify is

        not that the charge exists; it is that OG&E has specified nothing about what becomes of the money.

        Google’s observation that the Company will hold the funds at no cost is an argument for the

        carrying charges AARP requests in subpart (iv) above, not an argument for eliminating the charge.

        The disagreement among the parties over which customers should receive the credit is itself a

        consequence of OG&E’s failure to answer PUD Data Request 07-06(e). The charge was calculated

        against identified programs, and the specification AARP requests would apply it to them.


        2.      THE CUSTOMER CLASS PROTECTION CHARGE REQUIRES A DEFINED METHODOLOGY,
                THRESHOLD, FILING INTERVAL, BURDEN OF PROOF, AND AUDIT RIGHTS, AND A COST-OF-
                SERVICE STUDY FOR THE XLPL CLASS SHOULD BE FILED ON A DATE CERTAIN.

                The Customer Class Protection Charge is the provision on which OG&E's assurance to

        existing customers principally rests. It is set at $0.00 per kW-month at both service levels. On this

        record it has no trigger, no threshold, no methodology, no filing date and no audit rights.

                Asked to define what was meant by testimony that cost causation principles would be

        “reviewed often” and “enforced on an ongoing basis” — including the interval, who conducts the

        review, the data used, whether results are filed, any event triggering an off-interval review, the

        enforcement mechanism, the party responsible, the action following a finding of non-compliance,

        the timeframe for corrective action, and the provision supplying enforcement authority — OG&E

        responded that “the Commission and all stakeholders will have an opportunity to review OG&E's

        cost of service and associated rates in each base rate proceeding,” and that “Commission rate

        regulation is an iterative process that unfolds and occurs on an ongoing and prospective basis

        through individual rate proceedings.”14 None of the enumerated items were supplied.

                   A protection that depends entirely on a future proceeding OG&E is free to initiate or not,

        measured by a methodology that has not been described, against a threshold that has not been

        defined, is not a protection the Commission can enforce. AARP recommends that, as a condition

        of approval, the XLPL Tariff specify (a) the methodology for the with-and-without cost-of-service

        study, (b) a defined threshold at which an impact is deemed adverse, (c) an interval and filing date

        on which the study must be performed and filed, independent of OG&E's discretion to initiate a

        general rate case, (d) that OG&E bear the burden of producing and supporting the study, and (e)

        audit rights for PUD and review rights for all parties, including the right to offer alternative

        calculations. AARP further recommends that the Commission require OG&E to file a cost-of-

        service study for the XLPL class, together with proposed rates derived from that study, in its next

        general rate case or within a period certain following the date on which the first XLPL customer

        commences service, whichever occurs first.

                   PUD reaches the same conclusion. Although PUD finds that the filing contains reasonable

        structural protections, it “does not . . . ask the Commission to find that the filing as made discharges

        the cost-causation standard of 17 O.S. Section 902,” because the Application “does not supply the

        method by which cost causation will be measured.”15 PUD accordingly recommends that, as new

        generation, capacity, and energy costs are brought on board, “the cost of that new generation

        should be allocated to the XLPL class to the extent it is caused by XLPL load, rather than averaged

        across all classes with the Company’s embedded fleet.”16 The Attorney General’s witnesses ask

        for the same discipline from two directions. Mr. Beling would require “defined parameters and a

        clear methodology” for the fail-safe analysis, because “[i]f certain cost components or generation

        resources are not considered in the fail-safe analysis, the result will not represent the true impact

        allocation factors more frequently, because lagging allocators shift cost between classes in the

        interval.18 AARP supports each of these recommendations. Together they supply, in substance, the

        3.      THE PROCEEDS OF THE PROPOSED CUSTOMER CLASS PROTECTION CHARGE SHOULD
                BE PLACED IN A REGULATORY LIABILITY TO BE CREDITED TO NON -XLPL CUSTOMERS.

                These proceeds derived from the Customer Class Protection Charge should be treated in a

        manner comparable to the treatment proposed for the Customer Affordability Charge and the

        Reservation Charge, as described in OG&E Witness Shoop's Direct Testimony.19 OG&E has

        described that treatment: those revenues “will be recorded as a regulatory liability to be reviewed

        in a future rate proceeding” and “will be deferred to a regulatory liability on a monthly basis.” 20

        AARP recommends the same treatment for the Customer Class Protection Charge, subject to the

        crediting and carrying-charge requirements described in Recommendation 1 above.

        class deficiencies or surpluses.”21 Any adverse impact arising between the effective date of the

                On September 9, 2026, the stipulating parties in Cause No. PUD 2026-000031 filed a Joint

         charges,” reasoning that they “track a measured allocation effect rather than capital the Company

         5.      INACCURATE USE OF THE CONCEPT OF ECONOMIES OF SCALE.

                   It is not accurate to imply or suggest that the expansion of OG&E's load will generate

        economies of scale when that expansion is predicated on OG&E making new capital investments

        in order to meet that new demand for electric service. Economies of scale occur when a utility can

        serve additional load using existing plant and equipment, thus spreading the associated fixed costs

        across a larger number of customers. The key point is that economies of scale occur only if the

        load growth is based on existing, as opposed to incremental/additional, plant and equipment.

                   Where a tariff is designed to recover average embedded cost, and the incremental cost of

        the resources required to serve the new load exceeds that average, the difference is borne by the

        remaining classes. OG&E has neither quantified that difference nor identified who bears it.

        Indeed, OG&E has confirmed, “[t]he tariff is designed to recover average embedded cost of service

        with the exception of the Customer Protection Charge and Customer Affordability Charge,” and

        that “OG&E has not performed the requested quantification analysis” of the difference between

        the average embedded cost of service and the incremental cost of serving new large load. 28 In the

        same request, PUD asked OG&E to identify the specific provision of the Tariff recovering each of

        eight categories of cost incurred to serve large loads reliably, including incremental planning

        reserve margin, incremental accredited generating capacity, ancillary services, spinning and non-

                The Attorney General’s witness reaches the same conclusion by examining the Company’s

        own arithmetic. Mr. Lewis reviewed the modified cost-of-service analysis offered in Cause No.

        Company did not include any costs of serving the new load when conducting this analysis.”30 As

        he puts it: “The Company analysis included the new load but no new costs. In effect, the only

        possible result of the analysis would be a rate decrease because the analysis added load without

        adding any new cost.”31 Asked whether a utility such as OG&E can serve hundreds or thousands

        of megawatts of new load without incurring any cost, he answered that it cannot.32 AARP agrees,

        and recommends that the Commission decline to accept the characterization.
